§2.3a — Why do we have Seasons?

Unit 2: The Night Sky · Astronomy

Two photos of Earth from a camera parked between us and the Sun, six months apart. In June the Arctic is tipped into the light. In December it is gone, and Antarctica is lit all the way round. NASA EPIC Team

In Portland, July is hot and January is cold. In Chile it is the other way round. Is that because we are closer to the Sun in summer?

Today: what really causes the seasons, why the Sun's height matters, and the five circles of latitude the Sun draws on the Earth.

Which is correct? Proximity or tilt

Two ideas: (1) proximity, Earth's orbit brings us closer to the Sun in summer; (2) tilt (obliquity), Earth's axis is tipped $23.5^\circ$. Four reasons it can't be that we are closer to the Sun in the winter:

  1. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
  2. The Earth's orbit is only a few degrees off from a perfect circle.
  3. The Tropics are warm all year.
  4. The Seasons flip when you cross the equator.
Earth's orbit, drawn to scale

Measure: how much more sunlight in January?

Sunlight falls off as $\frac{1}{d^2}$. Earth is $1.47\times10^{11}$ m from the Sun on Jan 3 and $1.52\times10^{11}$ m on Jul 5. In relative form, how many times more sunlight does Earth get in January?

times

Tilt causes δ⊙ to change

Earth's axis always points at the same spot in the sky (the NCP, near Polaris) as Earth goes round the Sun. So for half the year the north is tipped toward the Sun, and for half the year away. Seen from Earth, the Sun slides along the ecliptic, and its declination swings from $\delta_\odot = +23.5^\circ$ to $-23.5^\circ$ and back.

Sun transits at different altitude

The Sun is a "star" whose declination changes. It still transits on the meridian at noon, at the height you know from §2.2a:

$\boxed{\theta_{\rm max} = 90^\circ - |{\rm lat} - \delta_\odot|}$
In the north, with the Sun south of the zenith, this is the same as $\theta = 90 - {\rm lat} + \delta$.

Anchorage, Alaska is at latitude $61^\circ$ N. How high is the noon Sun there on Jun 21?

°
Look up on Mon Nov 30. In Portland the Sun rises at 7:29 am, transits at 11:59 am only $23^\circ$ up, and sets at 4:29 pm: 9 hours of daylight. On Dec 21 it will be $21^\circ$ up at 12:08 pm, with 8 h 42 m of daylight. At noon, measure the shadow of a meter stick: on a low-Sun day it is more than twice the stick's length.

Why does altitude matter? Two effects

(1) Dilution. Shine a flashlight straight down: a small bright spot. Tip it: the same light spreads over a bigger, dimmer patch. A 1-m bundle of sunlight smears over $\frac{1\ {\rm m}}{\sin\theta}$ of ground. (2) Day length. With the axis tipped toward the Sun, more of each northern circle of latitude is in daylight: more hours of heating.

Special circles

The Sun draws five circles of latitude on the Earth. The tropics are where the Sun can go through the zenith. The polar circles are where the Sun can stay up all day, or not rise at all. Both are set by the tilt: tropics at $\pm 23.5^\circ$, polar circles at $\pm(90 - 23.5) = \pm 66.5^\circ$.

Sources and further reading

Want to dig deeper? Each title links straight to the original.

The data

  • NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis (NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory): the 30-year monthly averages (1991–2020) behind the temperature map.

Proximity or tilt

  • What causes the seasons? (NASA Space Place): a short explainer with animations.
  • Perihelion and aphelion (Wikipedia): Earth's closest and farthest points, with the dates.
  • EPIC: Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera (NASA): a new photo of the whole sunlit Earth every couple of hours. Compare June and December yourself.

The Sun's height and the special circles

  • Circles of latitude (Wikipedia): the equator, tropics and polar circles, and why they slowly move.
  • Midnight sun (Wikipedia): what it looks like and where you can see it.
  • Midnight sun, Chukchi Sea (USGS): the photo on this page, from a research ship in the Arctic.

Tonight's sky

  • Astronomy Engine (Don Cross): the code that computed Portland's sunrise, noon Sun and the perihelion date.
  • Natural Earth: the coastlines on the maps and globes.
